title: Diagnose the Field Samples
instructions: Look over each leaf with the zoom scope (1× to 20×) and mark the symptoms you find: some only show at high magnification. Then look closer under the microscope, focus it and mark what you see. Finally, identify what is causing the problem.

findings.name: Large dead area (necrosis, blight)
findings.description: Brown, dead tissue spreading from the leaf stem: necrosis, shown as a blight.
findings.clue: Start near the leaf stem, at the top right of the leaf.

findings.name: Dark lesion beside the midrib
findings.description: A dark brown lesion of dead tissue (necrosis), with discolouration around it.
findings.clue: Follow the midrib down to the middle of the leaf.

findings.name: Lower dark lesion
findings.description: Another dark lesion: the blight is spreading down the leaf.
findings.clue: Look at the lower half of the leaf, just left of the midrib.

findings.name: Pale trail on the leaf edge
findings.decoyMessage: That is not a late blight symptom: it looks like a leaf-miner track or a tear.

findings.name: Spore masses at the lesion edge (a sign)
findings.description: Spore masses where the dead tissue meets green leaf: something you see of the pathogen itself.
findings.clue: At the lower edge of the large dead area, where it meets green leaf. It only shows at 20×, as microscope detail.

rounds.question: Which pathogen group causes this disease?

choices.label: Oomycete
choices.description: Water mold; spreads in cool, wet weather

choices.label: Fungus
choices.description: Thread-like; spots, rusts, mildews; spreads by spores

choices.label: Bacterium
choices.description: Single-celled; leaf spots, blights, wilts; ooze in wet weather

choices.label: Virus
choices.description: Particles inside cells; mottling, curling, stunting

rounds.explanation: This is late blight of tomato. Its pathogen, Phytophthora infestans, is an oomycete (water mold): the pathogen is the organism, late blight is the disease it causes (Lesson 2.2). Oomycetes are an important pathogen group of their own, apart from the true fungi (Lesson 2.3). The symptoms are necrosis and blight — dead brown tissue spreading through the leaf — and the sign is the spore masses at the edge of the lesions.

rounds.question: What causes these symptoms?

choices.label: Fungus
choices.description: Thread-like; spots, rusts, mildews; spreads by spores

choices.label: Bacterium
choices.description: Single-celled; leaf spots, blights, wilts; ooze in wet weather

choices.label: Virus
choices.description: Particles inside cells; mottling, curling, stunting

rounds.explanation: Viruses are tiny particles that live inside plant cells and cause mottled, curled or stunted growth, and they are often spread by insects. Under the microscope the cells show light and dark (mosaic) patches but no fungal threads, spores or ooze — as in tungro-infected rice, the cause is a virus.

rounds.question: What causes these symptoms and signs?

choices.label: Fungus
choices.description: Thread-like; spots, rusts, mildews; spreads by spores

choices.label: Bacterium
choices.description: Single-celled; leaf spots, blights, wilts; ooze in wet weather

choices.label: Virus
choices.description: Particles inside cells; mottling, curling, stunting

rounds.explanation: Fungi are thread-like organisms that cause spots, rusts, mildews, rots and wilts, and they spread by spores. Under the microscope the lesion shows fungal threads (mycelium) and spores — signs of the pathogen — so the cause is a fungus, as in rice blast lesions.

rounds.explanation: Bacteria are single-celled organisms that cause leaf spots, blights, wilts and soft rots, especially in wet conditions. Bacterial ooze — a sticky or milky liquid from cut or diseased tissue — is a sign of bacteria, and under the microscope the single cells stream out of the cut tissue.
